content.title: About
content.content: Collard greens are a leafy vegetable from the Brassicaceae family, originally cultivated in the Mediterranean region. Fresh leaves are typically cooked by steaming, boiling, or simmering without added fat, preserving their bright green color and crisp texture. Collards are rich in vitamins, minerals, and dietary fiber.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Collards belong to the same family as cabbage, broccoli, and Brussels sprouts.
Leaves can grow up to 60 cm long, and stalks may reach 1.5 m.
In traditional Southern U.S. cuisine collards are often served with smoked meat, but they can be prepared fat‑free by simply boiling in salted water.
High chlorophyll content makes them an excellent source of antioxidants.
Collards are frequently used in children’s meals because their mild flavor is well accepted.

items.title: Rich in vitamin K
items.content: One cup of cooked collard greens provides over 800 % of the daily value for vitamin K, essential for blood clotting and bone health.

items.title: High in vitamin A
items.content: Beta‑carotene in the leaves converts to vitamin A, supporting vision and immune function.

items.title: Source of vitamin C
items.content: Vitamin C adds antioxidant protection and enhances iron absorption.

items.title: Mineral dense
items.content: Collards contain calcium, iron, magnesium, and potassium, which are important for muscle, nerve, and electrolyte balance.

items.title: Dietary fiber
items.content: Fiber promotes healthy digestion, satiety, and helps regulate blood sugar levels.

items.title: Oxalates
items.content: Collard greens contain oxalates that may contribute to kidney stone formation in susceptible individuals.

items.title: Interaction with anticoagulants
items.content: Large amounts of vitamin K can reduce the effectiveness of blood‑thinning medications.

items.title: Pesticide residues
items.content: As with many leafy greens, collards may carry pesticide residues; thorough washing before cooking is recommended.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Collard greens can be boiled in salted water for 5‑7 minutes, steamed, or quickly sautéed without oil using a splash of broth. They are added to soups, stews, salads, and smoothies. For a milder taste, soak the leaves in cold water before cooking.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store fresh leaves in a bag or container in the refrigerator for up to 5 days. Cooked portions can be frozen in airtight bags for up to 3 months.
